issues.legal_issue: Land held by a member of a family unit must be included in the unit’s holding for ceiling purposes regardless of whether it is that member’s separate or stridhan property.
material_facts: The respondent’s wife held land in her own name, which the respondent claimed was her separate property.
The Tribunal included the wife’s land in the family unit’s total holding when determining whether it exceeded the ceiling.
The respondent, his wife, and their minor children fell within the statutory definition of a family unit.
issues.conclusion: All land held by each member of the family unit, jointly or separately, must be pooled when determining the unit’s ceiling holding; the character of a member’s interest in the land is irrelevant.
issues.legal_principle: Section 4(1) of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, deems all land held by each member of a family unit to be held by the unit for determining its ceiling area. The Explanation defines a family unit to include a person, the person’s spouse, and their minor sons and minor unmarried daughters. Read with sections 3(1) and 3(2), which prohibit holdings above the ceiling and treat excess land as surplus, the provision requires aggregation whether land is held jointly or separately. No earlier cases are relied on.

predicates.family_unit_ceiling_case: The proceeding determines the permissible landholding of a family unit under an agricultural land ceiling regime.
predicates.land_held_by_unit_member: A person within the family unit held land, whether jointly or separately.
predicates.separate_or_stridhan_claim: A party claimed that land held by a family-unit member was that member’s separate or stridhan property.

issues.definition: When a family-unit ceiling proceeding concerns land held by a unit member, a claim that the land is separate or stridhan property does not prevent its inclusion with the unit’s other land.

issues.legal_issue: A reviewing court may not enlarge a limited remand to require inquiry into whether a family-unit member’s land is separate property when that character does not affect the ceiling calculation.
material_facts: The Additional Commissioner remanded the matter for inquiry into whether the wife’s post-notification sale of land was supported by legal necessity.
The High Court enlarged the remand to require an additional inquiry into whether the land held in the wife’s name was her separate property.
The Supreme Court held that separate-property status was irrelevant to aggregating land for the family-unit ceiling.
issues.conclusion: The High Court’s expanded remand was set aside, and the Tribunal was directed to conduct only the inquiry specified in the Additional Commissioner’s remand.
issues.legal_principle: Because section 4(1) of the Maharashtra Agricultural Lands (Ceiling on Holdings) Act, 1961, requires all land held by members of the family unit to be aggregated regardless of the nature of their interests, an inquiry into whether the wife’s land was separate property was immaterial. The Court confirmed the original remand’s limited scope; it relied on no earlier cases.

predicates.appeal_against_expanded_remand: A party appealed from a reviewing court’s order that enlarged the scope of an administrative remand.
predicates.original_remand_limited_to_sale_necessit: The original remand required inquiry into whether a land sale was supported by legal necessity.
predicates.added_inquiry_concerns_irrelevant_proper: The added remand inquiry concerned whether land held by a family-unit member was separate property, a matter irrelevant to calculating the unit’s ceiling holding.

issues.definition: When an appeal challenges an expanded remand, the original remand is limited to its stated inquiry if the added inquiry concerns a property characteristic that does not affect the relevant determination.
